summary: Reports on the IAB workshop on Barriers to Internet Access of Services, held online in January 2024. Based on position papers, it covered community networks, the digital divide, and related topics.

eli5.summary: A group of internet experts met to talk about why some people struggle to use online services, and wrote down what they said.

questions: barriers to internet access of services
subtitle: Reports on barriers to internet access including community networks, digital divide, and censorship.

tldr.problem: Despite growing internet infrastructure, significant barriers prevent equal access to services, including community network management gaps, digital inequalities in service provisioning, and government censorship in various regions.
tldr.mechanism: An IAB workshop held in January 2024 brought together experts to discuss three key areas: community networks as alternative connectivity providers, disparities in digital access across populations, and censorship measurement and circumvention.
tldr.outcome: The workshop identified actionable takeaways including the need for better community network documentation, protocol enhancements for transparency on filtering and privacy protection, and coordination with existing IETF research groups on access and rights issues.

today: RFC 9707 is an Informational RFC published in February 2025 and has not been obsoleted. It serves as a reference document for current barriers to internet access and recommendations for future IETF work.

sections.title: Workshop Overview and Scope
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) convenes workshops to consider long-term issues affecting the Internet's future. This January 2024 workshop focused on barriers to internet access of services (BIAS), recognizing that simply having internet connectivity is not enough to achieve meaningful access to digital infrastructure and services.

The workshop organized discussions around three main topics: the role of community networks in providing internet access to underserved areas; evidence of the digital divide in service provisioning, language support, and web affordability; and measurements of internet censorship practices with analysis of censorship circumvention methods like VPNs.
sections.eli5: A group of internet leaders met to talk about different reasons why people might struggle to use the internet even when they are connected.

sections.title: Community Networks and Connectivity
sections.content:
Community networks are self-organized, locally owned networks that provide internet access to areas where commercial internet service providers lack economic incentive. The workshop covered their crucial role in closing connectivity gaps, but also identified challenges.

Key issues discussed included the inconsistent quality of service in community deployments due to varying operator expertise, the high cost of transit and internet services that make it difficult for community networks to scale, the role of satellite internet in rural access, and spectrum allocation conflicts between community networks and commercial 5G deployment in bands like the 6 GHz range.

Participants emphasized the need for better documentation of best practices, explicit manageability considerations in future protocol designs, and greater involvement of community network operators in the IETF and IRTF.
sections.eli5: Local communities sometimes build their own networks to reach people that regular internet companies cannot serve. But they need help with tools, training, and getting access to the radio frequencies to transmit.

sections.title: Digital Divide and Service Access
sections.content:
The digital divide extends beyond simple connectivity: even when users have internet access, inequality persists in the services available to them. The workshop examined three specific dimensions of this problem.

Service provisioning disparities: Research on DNS dependencies showed different configurations for Indigenous populations in Australia compared to the general population, suggesting differential treatment in government service access. Language and script support: While internationalized domain names (IDNs) and multilingual email addresses are technically standardized, software and applications have not yet universally adopted these scripts, limiting who can use localized domain names. Web affordability: As websites grow in complexity and file size, the monetary cost to end users—especially those paying per-gigabyte—rises significantly, creating a barrier in regions with high mobile broadband prices and lower incomes.
sections.eli5: Even when people have the internet, they might face unfairness: fewer government services in their language, websites so big and expensive that they cannot afford to use them, or services that are just not available to them.

sections.title: Censorship and Circumvention
sections.content:
The workshop documented widespread internet censorship across multiple regions. Measurements from Cambodia, Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Thailand, Timor-Leste, Vietnam, Pakistan, and Russia revealed blocking of content through DNS tampering, HTTP tampering, and Server Name Indication (SNI) filtering. Blocking is often implemented inconsistently across different ISPs and may show or hide block pages depending on the jurisdiction and method used.

Discussion of censorship circumvention highlighted both the prevalence and fragility of VPN services: while VPNs help users bypass censorship, many commercial VPN services have security shortcomings that leak DNS traffic, IPv6 traffic, or non-browser traffic, failing to meet user expectations for privacy and anonymity. The workshop noted a cat-and-mouse game between censorship technologies and circumvention tools, requiring continued protocol enhancements for privacy.
sections.eli5: Many countries block websites their governments do not like. People use VPNs to tunnel around these blocks, but those tools are not always as safe or private as users think.

sections.title: Recommendations and Future Work
sections.content:
The workshop identified seven key takeaways for the internet community. The technical community should address management gaps in community networks and document best practices for their operation. Future protocol development should explicitly consider manageability for community networks, not just large-scale deployment.

Consensus-driven solutions to digital inclusion are needed, moving beyond research and measurement to policy and deployment. Protocols should be enhanced to provide user privacy and to enable more transparency on filtering activities. The community could develop new VPN-like services and support measurements of their deployment. Related work was suggested for the GAIA, HRPC, PEARG, MAPRG research groups, OPSAWG, or potentially a new group focused on censorship.
sections.eli5: The experts suggested that the internet community should help build better tools for local networks, protect people's privacy, make services fairer and more affordable, and measure how well censorship blocking really works.
